drivers.contract: Confirmed for 2027; end date beyond 2027 not published (The Race lists his earlier deal as running to 2026)
drivers.bio: Scouted by Mercedes as a karter, the son of sportscar racer Marco Antonelli won the Italian and ADAC F4 titles in 2022 and both the Formula Regional Middle East and European crowns in 2023. Mercedes fast-tracked him straight to Formula 2 for 2024, skipping F3, and he won a wet Silverstone sprint and a Hungaroring feature race. Named Lewis Hamilton's replacement at 18, he debuted at the 2025 Australian GP by climbing from 16th to fourth, and finished his rookie year with three podiums and 150 points. [1][2][3][4]
drivers.season: Antonelli has been the dominant force of 2026, with nine grand prix wins from 18 rounds (China, Japan, Miami, Canada, Monaco, Belgium, Italy, Spain and the United States) and 15 podiums. Along the way he became F1's youngest polesitter (China) and youngest championship leader (Japan), took a grand chelem in Monaco during a run of five straight wins, and won at Monza from 19th on the grid after a power-unit penalty. His setbacks were an engine failure in Barcelona, a mechanical problem that left him 15th at Silverstone, and a qualifying error in Baku that put him 16th on the grid (he recovered to fifth). Victory in Austin took him to 365 points, 123 clear of team-mate George Russell with five rounds left, though the title was not sealed in Texas. [1][2][3][4]
drivers.best: Winner (9 times): China, Japan, Miami, Canada, Monaco, Belgium, Italy, Spain (Madrid), United States
drivers.h2h: vs Russell: GP qualifying 11-7, GP races 13-5 (Sky Sports, after US GP)
drivers.next: Mercedes has confirmed it is keeping Antonelli alongside Russell for 2027 (announced ahead of the British GP; listed as confirmed by GPFans on 20 Oct). [1][2][3][4]

drivers.bio: A Mercedes junior from 2017, Russell won the GP3 title that year and the Formula 2 crown in 2018. He spent three seasons at Williams from 2019, out-qualifying Robert Kubica at every race of his rookie year, and stood out when he replaced Lewis Hamilton at the 2020 Sakhir GP, missing pole by 0.026s. He scored his first Williams points and podium in 2021, then joined Mercedes and won in Brazil in 2022, the team's only victory that year. After Hamilton left for Ferrari he led Mercedes in 2025, winning twice. [1][2][3][4]
drivers.season: Russell opened the year with pole and victory in Australia and has since won in Austria and Azerbaijan, collecting eight podiums, five grand prix poles and three sprint wins. His campaign has been uneven: he retired in Canada, Belgium and the Bahrain GP at Sepang, finished 12th in Monaco, and in Singapore crashed in the sprint and then started the grand prix from the back after an engine penalty. He is second on 242 points, one ahead of Lewis Hamilton but 123 behind team-mate Antonelli, who leads their race head-to-head 13-5. He finished eighth in Austin. [1][2][3][4]

drivers.next: Retained by Mercedes alongside Antonelli for 2027; speculation that Verstappen could take his seat ended when Verstappen extended with Red Bull (GPFans). [1][2][3][4]

drivers.bio: Norris swept a string of junior titles: the 2015 MSA Formula championship, the 2016 Eurocup Formula Renault 2.0, Formula Renault NEC and Toyota Racing Series, and the 2017 European F3 crown. McLaren promoted him for 2019 and he debuted in Australia, took a maiden podium in 2020 and his first win in 2024, the year McLaren won its first constructors' title since 1998. In 2025 he won seven races and overturned a 34-point deficit to win the world championship, beating Oscar Piastri and Max Verstappen. [1][2][3][4]
drivers.season: Racing with the No. 1 as champion, Norris has won twice, in Hungary and the Netherlands (both from pole), added a third pole in Madrid and won the Miami sprint. He has five grand prix podiums, but reliability has hurt him: an electrical problem stopped him starting in China, a gearbox failure ended his race in Canada and a battery problem did the same in Monaco, and he also failed to finish in Baku. He also took a ten-place grid penalty at Spa. He is sixth on 211 points, well clear of Piastri, after fifth in Austin. [1][2][3][4]
drivers.best: Winner: Hungarian GP and Dutch GP

drivers.bio: Piastri won the 2019 Formula Renault Eurocup, then took the FIA F3 title in 2020 and the 2021 Formula 2 crown as a rookie, both with Prema. With Alpine and McLaren both claiming his services, he joined McLaren and debuted at the 2023 Bahrain GP, scoring two podiums that season. He won in Hungary and Azerbaijan in 2024 as McLaren took the constructors' title, then won seven races in 2025 and led the standings for much of the year before losing the title to Norris at the Abu Dhabi finale. [1][2][3][4]
drivers.season: Piastri's year began with two non-starts: he crashed on his reconnaissance lap in Australia after a sudden power surge over a kerb, and an electrical fault stopped him before the formation lap in China. He bounced back with second at Suzuka and third in Miami but has not been on the podium since, and in Hungary he led laps before contact with Carlos Sainz and a gearbox failure ended his race. He is seventh on 144 points without a win, and The Race's mid-season review judged he had adapted less well than Norris to the 2026 cars. He finished seventh in Austin. [1][2][3][4]

drivers.bio: The son of former F1 driver Jos Verstappen won world and European karting titles in 2013 and the 2014 Masters of F3, then debuted for Toro Rosso at the 2015 Australian GP aged 17, the youngest driver ever to start a grand prix. Promoted to Red Bull in 2016, he won on his first outing for the team in Barcelona to become F1's youngest winner. He won four straight titles from 2021 to 2024, including a record 19 wins in 2023, and missed a fifth by two points in 2025. [1][2][3][4]
drivers.season: Red Bull's first season with its own Red Bull Ford power unit started slowly: Verstappen crashed out in Q1 in Australia, retired with a coolant leak in China and spun on the opening lap in Miami. He has been on the podium at every race he has finished since Austria, and won the Bahrain GP (held at Sepang in Malaysia) and then Singapore, a race he had never won before. He has ten podiums and two poles but four retirements, and is fourth on 236 points after third in Austin. He has dominated his team-mates, leading Hadjar 11-4 in qualifying and stand-in Lawson 3-0. [1][2][3][4]

drivers.bio: A Red Bull junior from 2022, Hadjar never won a junior title, but he finished fourth in the 2022 FIA F3 standings with three wins and was runner-up in the 2024 Formula 2 championship with four victories. His Racing Bulls debut at the 2025 Australian GP ended before the start when he spun into the barriers on the formation lap. He recovered to score 51 points as a rookie, including a maiden podium at Zandvoort, and was promoted to partner Max Verstappen for 2026. [1][2][3][4]
drivers.season: Hadjar's first Red Bull season has been eventful. He qualified third in Australia before an engine failure, was disqualified from Miami qualifying and crashed out early from a pit-lane start, then took his first Red Bull podium in Monaco, where third place was confirmed only after appeals over Pierre Gasly's penalty. A wrist fracture suffered in training over the summer break kept him out of the Dutch, Italian and Madrid rounds. He returned with third in Baku and has since added fifth at Sepang, tenth in Singapore and sixth in Austin, and is eighth on 105 points. [1][2][3][4]

Ferrari promoted him for 2019 and he won at Spa and then at Monza a week later, out-scoring Sebastian Vettel over the season. drivers.season: Leclerc started well with podiums in Australia and Japan, but a difficult run from Montreal to Barcelona, with brake complaints and retirements in Monaco and Barcelona, led Ferrari to change brake-disc supplier. He recovered to win the British GP and has added second places in Belgium, Singapore and Austin, for six podiums in all. He also retired on the opening lap at Monza and is fifth on 233 points, eight behind Hamilton, in an almost dead-level intra-team fight. [1][2][3][4]

drivers.bio: Lawson won New Zealand's Formula Ford championship and the 2019 Toyota Racing Series, then was a front-runner in F3 and F2 as a Red Bull junior. He debuted for AlphaTauri in place of the injured Daniel Ricciardo at the rain-hit 2023 Dutch GP, and in Singapore that year out-qualified Max Verstappen and scored points. Promoted to Red Bull for 2025 in place of Sergio Pérez, he was sent back to Racing Bulls after only two races. [1][2][3][4]
drivers.season: Lawson has been Racing Bulls' lead driver, scoring regularly with a best of fifth in Monaco and sixth at Silverstone, and his only retirement came in Miami. When Hadjar broke his wrist he stepped up to Red Bull for three races, finishing seventh at Zandvoort, 14th at Monza after an engine-change grid penalty and front-wing damage, and sixth in Madrid. Back at Racing Bulls he took seventh at Sepang and Singapore and ninth in Austin, and he is ninth on 77 points. He leads rookie team-mate Lindblad 9-6 in qualifying and 11-4 in races. [1][2][3][4]

drivers.bio: Alonso won a string of Spanish karting titles and the 1999 Euro Open by Nissan before debuting for Minardi at the 2001 Australian GP. With Renault he became, at the time, the youngest polesitter, winner and world champion, taking back-to-back titles in 2005 and 2006, and he later raced for McLaren, Ferrari and Alpine. He also won Le Mans twice, took eight podiums in his first Aston Martin season in 2023, and became the first driver to reach 400 grand prix starts. [1][2][3][4]
drivers.season: Aston Martin's Honda-powered AMR26 has been slow and unreliable, and Alonso retired from the first two races before finishing 18th in Japan. He scored the team's first points with tenth in Monaco, helped by penalties to cars ahead, and added ninth at Zandvoort and eighth at Sepang, the team's only points of the year. He has six retirements and is 17th on seven points, but he has dominated Stroll, out-qualifying him 16-2. He finished 16th in Austin. [1][2][3][4]

drivers.bio: Colapinto won the 2019 Spanish F4 title and joined the Williams academy in 2023. He debuted for Williams at the 2024 Italian GP in place of Logan Sargeant, the first Argentine in F1 for 23 years. After starting 2025 as Alpine's reserve he replaced Jack Doohan from round seven and kept the seat for 2026. [1][2][3][4]
drivers.season: Colapinto's first full season has been inconsistent but productive, with a career-best sixth in Canada, seventh in Miami and Madrid, and several tenth places. He took a stop-and-go penalty for a start infringement in Australia and has retired three times, in Baku, Singapore and Austin. He is 12th on 27 points and has been clearly behind Gasly in qualifying, though their race battle is closer at 7-10. [1][2][3][4]
drivers.h2h: vs Gasly: GP qualifying 3-15, GP races 7-10 (Sky Sports, after US GP)
drivers.next: Confirmed at Alpine for 2027. [1][2][3][4]

drivers.bio: Pérez won the national class of British F3 in 2007 and debuted for Sauber at the 2011 Australian GP, where both Saubers were later disqualified. After spells at McLaren and Force India/Racing Point he won the 2020 Sakhir GP, then joined Red Bull and added five more wins as Max Verstappen's team-mate, becoming Mexico's highest-scoring F1 driver. After a year out in 2025 he returned with the new Cadillac team. [1][2][3][4]
drivers.season: Cadillac has yet to score in its debut season, and Pérez's best result is 14th, which he achieved in Barcelona, at Silverstone and in Baku. He has retired five times, collided with Bottas in China, and made grid-parking errors in Monaco that The Race said cost the team its first point. He has generally been Cadillac's reference driver, leading Bottas 10-8 in qualifying and 12-4 in races. He was 19th in Austin. [1][2][3][4]
drivers.h2h: vs Bottas: GP qualifying 10-8, GP races 12-4 (Sky Sports, after US GP)
drivers.next: Listed as confirmed at Cadillac for 2027 (GPFans, 20 Oct), though a GPFans headline says the team boss would not confirm the Pérez and Bottas 2027 contracts; in August he was linked with Williams. [1][2][3][4]

drivers.bio: Bottas won the 2008 Formula Renault Eurocup and NEC titles and the 2011 GP3 crown, and debuted for Williams at the 2013 Australian GP. He replaced Nico Rosberg at Mercedes in 2017 and won ten races there, finishing runner-up in the 2019 championship. After three seasons with Alfa Romeo/Sauber and a year as Mercedes reserve in 2025, he returned to racing with Cadillac. [1][2][3][4]
drivers.season: Bottas has had a punishing return, failing to finish nine of 18 races, with brake problems in Monaco and Hungary, overheating in Barcelona, a brake fire on lap two in Austria and a hydraulic fault at Zandvoort. His best result is 13th in China, and he is still without a point, 22nd in the standings. The Race said team problems held him back and some mistakes cost him results, and Pérez leads their race head-to-head 12-4. He retired again in Austin. [1][2][3][4]
drivers.h2h: vs Pérez: GP qualifying 8-10, GP races 4-12 (Sky Sports, after US GP)
drivers.next: Listed as confirmed for 2027, but GPFans described him as under pressure in August and reported that the Cadillac boss would not confirm the 2027 contracts; its 20 Oct update says he appears set to stay. [1][2][3][4]

market.text: With five rounds left, 19 of the 22 seats for 2027 are filled; the only vacancies are both Racing Bulls cars and the second Haas seat (GPFans, 20 Oct). The summer brought a wave of long-term deals: Max Verstappen extended with Red Bull to 2030, ending talk of a move to McLaren or Mercedes; Lando Norris re-signed with McLaren to 2030; Charles Leclerc signed a long extension with Ferrari; Williams tied Carlos Sainz to a multi-year deal; and Alpine kept Franco Colapinto. Red Bull renewed Isack Hadjar for 2027 on his return from injury, Mercedes kept Kimi Antonelli and George Russell together, and Fernando Alonso, 45, extended with Aston Martin through 2027 rather than retire. The one confirmed newcomer is Rafael Câmara, Ferrari's 21-year-old Brazilian junior and F2 leader, who signed with Haas on 15 October to replace Esteban Ocon; Oliver Bearman is widely expected to stay alongside him, but his deal had not been formally announced. Racing Bulls boss Alan Permane says the team will choose two of Liam Lawson, rookie Arvid Lindblad and F2 title contender Nikola Tsolov in the coming weeks; RacingNews365 reports that Lawson would be the one at risk if Tsolov is promoted, while GPFans now calls a Tsolov call-up highly unlikely. Ocon calls himself a free agent and would accept a reserve role, while Yuki Tsunoda was reported by Motorsport.com to be in talks with Meyer Shank Racing for an IndyCar seat. Cadillac's Sergio Pérez and Valtteri Bottas are listed as contracted for 2027, although GPFans reported that the team boss would not confirm their deals. [1][2][3][4]
